content: 1. The Arab Resource Collective Director is affiliated with the Arab Network for Early Childhood Care and Development, based in Beirut, Lebanon. 2. Steward Kabaka serves as the focal person for Early Childhood Development at the Ministry of Health in Nairobi, Kenya. 3. Betty Kirkwood is a Professor of Epidemiology and International Health, specializing in maternal and child health interventions, at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine in London, United Kingdom. 4. Vibha Krishnamurthy is the Founder and Executive Director of the Ummeed Child Development Center in Mumbai, India. 5. Kofi Marfo is a Professor and the Founding Director of the Institute for Human Development at Aga Khan University in Nairobi, Kenya. 6. Joerg Meerpohl, a methodologist, is affiliated with the University Medical Centre Freiburg in Germany. 7. Linda Richter is a Distinguished Professor at the DSI-NRF Centre of Excellence in Human Development at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa. 8. Mark Tomlinson is a Professor at the Institute for Life Course Health Research at Stellenbosch University in Stellenbosch, South Africa. 9. Susan Walker is a Professor of Nutrition at the Tropical Medicine Research Institute, University of the West Indies, Kingston, Jamaica. 10. Joshua Jeong and Emily Franchett are both affiliated with the Department of Global Health and Population at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, MA, United States. 11. Aisha Yousafzai, also from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, has contributed to WHO recommendations on psychotherapeutic interventions for maternal mental health issues to improve early childhood development in lowand middle-income countries. 12. Atif Rahman is affiliated with the Human Development Research Foundation in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, and the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom. 13. Jane Fisher is a faculty member at the School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Monash University, Melbourne, Australia. 14. Ahmed Waqas is associated with the Human Development Research Foundation in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, and CMH Lahore Medical College & Institute of Dentistry in Lahore Cantt, Pakistan. 15. Syed Usman Hamdani is affiliated with the Human Development Research Foundation in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, and the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom. 16. Wajeeha Zafar, Nadia Suleman, and Zill-e-Huma are all members of the Human Development Research Foundation in Rawalpindi, Pakistan. 17. Renee Zeng, Sara Holton, and Minh Le are faculty members at the School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, Monash University, Melbourne, Australia. 18. Frances Aboud, from McGill University in Canada, has received consultancy payments from UNICEF, the Aga Khan Foundation, and the Brookings Institution. 19. Jane Fisher, in her capacity as the Jean Hailes Professor of Women’s Health at Monash University and as President of the International Marce Society for Perinatal Health, has received funding for her work. 20. Subodh Gupta, based in India, received research funding from the WHO country office. 21. Vibha Krishnamurthy, also from India, received a research grant from the National Institute of Health, USA, for the development of an international guide to monitor and support child development. 22. Linda Richter, from the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa, received a research grant from the Conrad Hilton Foundation to review guidance on programs supporting young children affected by HIV and AIDS. 23. Mark Tomlinson, from Stellenbosch University, South Africa, received research funding from the Hilton Foundation. 24. Aisha Yousafzai, from Harvard University, USA, has received funding from Grand Challenges Canada and travel support from WHO for consultancy work. 25. The WHO guideline on improving early childhood development includes recommendations on caregiving interventions to support socioemotional and behavioral development in children under three years of age. 26. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of psychotherapeutic interventions for maternal mental health problems in lowand middle-income countries. 27. Evidence from studies shows mixed results, with some reporting significant positive impacts on child outcomes, while others found no effects or null results. 28. Integrated caregiving and nutrition interventions have been compared to standard care, with varying results in terms of child development outcomes. 29. Studies often report wide confidence intervals (CIs) around pooled estimates, indicating variability in the magnitude and direction of effects. 30. Many studies included in the reviews have small sample sizes, which limits the generalizability of findings. 31. Subgroup analyses have been used to explain heterogeneity in outcomes, particularly in interventions combining nutrition and caregiving. 32. The certainty of evidence for various outcomes ranges from low to moderate, depending on the quality and consistency of the studies. 33. Exclusive breastfeeding interventions have been evaluated, with some studies reporting significant improvements in child outcomes, while others found no effects. 34. Other interventions targeting maternal mental health include elements such as parent-child interaction, communication skills, nutrition, caregiver coping, social support, and behavioral contracting. 35. The overall certainty of evidence is often downgraded due to imprecision, heterogeneity, and the small number of studies contributing to pooled estimates.
